transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I feel like I can’t keep the moving parts organized anymore. I’ve got patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—all these things competing—and instead of doing what actually matters most, I end up just starting with whatever is loudest or most urgent in the moment. It’s been getting hard to manage.

Has this difficulty organizing and prioritizing tasks been a pattern for you since childhood or adolescence, or is this something that started more recently in response to a particular change or stressor in your life?

It goes back pretty far, yeah. Looking back, it was there in grade school. Teachers would write that I was bright, but I daydreamed a lot, or I’d forget to turn in assignments even when I’d actually done them. I also remember losing homework folders pretty regularly, well before I was a teenager.
Aside from feeling overwhelmed by competing tasks, do you find yourself worrying excessively about various things—work, health, relationships—in a way that's hard to control, on most days?

I’m not really sure I’d describe it as excessive worrying, no. I do get stressed when there’s a lot going on, but it’s more like I lose track of what to do first than sitting there worrying about every area of my life most days.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling consistently down, sad, or empty, or noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you'd normally enjoy, most of the day, nearly every day?
No, I don’t think so. I get frustrated and stressed, but I haven’t been feeling down or empty most of the day, and I’m still interested in things I normally enjoy.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong (since grade school) pattern of difficulty organizing and prioritizing tasks, distractibility (daydreaming), and losing important items (homework folders), consistent with predominantly inattentive-type symptoms. These difficulties are chronic, began before adolescence, and are not better explained by excessive generalized worry (GAD ruled out) or a mood episode (depression ruled out, as pervasive low mood/anhedonia was denied). The clinical picture supports ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
